entry.title: OpenAI CLIP Source Tour: Inside the Dual Encoder That Learned to Match Images and Words

link.title: OpenAI CLIP Source Tour: Inside the Dual Encoder That Learned to Match Images and Words

entry.content:
When OpenAI released CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) in January 2021, the accompanying paper made a claim that sounded almost careless: train on 400 million (image, text) pairs scraped from the web, and the resulting model can name things it was never explicitly taught. The headline demo was zero-shot ImageNet classification — matching the performance of a ResNet-50 trained on all 1.28 million labeled examples, without ever seeing one of those labels. What is more interesting for readers of this series is the artifact itself: the released repository is tiny. One model file, one loader, one tokenizer, and a gzipped vocabulary. No training code, no data loaders for the 400-million-pair corpus, no experiment framework. Just the trained dual encoder and the minimum scaffolding needed to run it.

The idea is easier to state than to train. Two encoders run side by side: an image encoder (either a modified ResNet or a Vision Transformer) and a text encoder (a masked self-attention stack in the GPT-2 family, architecturally a cousin of the models covered in our /transformers/ tour). Each encoder projects into a shared embedding space of identical width. During training, a batch of N image-text pairs produces an N-by-N matrix of cosine similarities, and a symmetric cross-entropy loss pushes the N correct pairings toward 1 while suppressing the N-squared-minus-N wrong ones. At inference, any string can stand in for a class name, and classification becomes a similarity lookup. If you have followed our /nanogpt/ tour, the text side will feel immediately familiar: token embedding, learned positional embedding, causal multi-head attention, QuickGELU MLPs.

The public surface is deliberately narrow. clip.available_models(), clip.load(), clip.tokenize() — three functions, nine checkpoints, one preprocessing chain built from the same torchvision primitives we walked in our /torchvision/ tour, and a byte-pair-encoding tokenizer that anticipates the modern wave of tokenizer tooling we covered in our /tokenizers/ tour. This post walks the actual files on main with line-verified anchors, then closes with the trade-offs the authors wrote down.

Repository flow of openai/CLIP: the package API in clip/clip.py feeds build_model in clip/model.py, the dual-encoder definition; clip/simple_tokenizer.py loads the gzipped BPE vocabulary; setup.py, the CI workflow and the consistency test hold the packaging and verification perimeter.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • load, L94 — the single entry point: resolves a model name or local checkpoint path, downloads with a SHA-256 gate, and returns (model, preprocess).
  • _MODELS, L30 — a flat dict of nine checkpoint URLs (RN50 through ViT-L/14@336px); each URL embeds its own checksum as the second-to-last segment.
  • build_model, L399 — reconstructs every hyperparameter from checkpoint tensor shapes, so no config file ever ships with a model.
  • CLIP, L243 — the dual-encoder wrapper that owns both towers, the projections, and the learned logit scale.
  • VisionTransformer, L206 — the image tower for ViT variants: patch-conv embedding, class token, transformer, and a learned projection to the joint space.
  • Transformer, L195 — the shared residual-attention stack, instantiated once for text and again (maskless) inside the ViT.
  • SimpleTokenizer, L62 — the byte-level BPE tokenizer whose entire vocabulary lives in one gzip file next to the code.
  • tokenize, L205 — wraps raw text into start-of-text / end-of-text tokens and pads every sequence to the fixed 77-token context.
  • test_consistency, L9 — the one test that matters: JIT and eager loads of every model must agree on softmax probabilities.

Why Contrastive Pretraining Is the Whole Trick

Everything CLIP does at inference is a consequence of how CLIP.forward, L358 is written. Both towers encode their inputs, each feature vector is L2-normalized along the batch dimension, and the logits are nothing more than a scaled matrix product: logit_scale * image_features @ text_features.t(). There is no classifier head anywhere. The logit scale, L295 is a learned scalar initialized to ln(1/0.07) ≈ 2.66 — an exponential temperature of about 14.3 — because raw cosine similarities in [-1, 1] are far too flat to drive a softmax over thousands of negatives.

That design is what makes zero-shot transfer work. To classify an image into K categories, you do not load new weights; you encode K caption templates with the same text tower used during training and pick the argmax row. The paper’s ablations showed the prompt wording matters enormously, which is why the repository ships data/prompts.md — the exact classes-and-templates used for 26 of the 27 zero-shot datasets in the paper, with the 80-template ImageNet ensemble relegated to a notebook.

Inside model.py: Two Encoders, One Joint Space

The smartest few lines in the repository are at the top of build_model, L399. The loader never carries an architecture config; instead the function interrogates the state dict. If "visual.proj" is present, the image tower is a ViT and the code reads width, patch size, and layer count straight out of tensor shapes — vision_patch_size from visual.conv1.weight.shape[-1], the grid from the positional-embedding length, and the transformer depth by counting distinct attn.in_proj_weight keys. Otherwise the tower is a ResNet and the counts come from the visual.layer{1..4} key groups. Every dimension, including the joint embed_dim and the 77-token context, is inferred rather than declared.

The ViT tower itself, VisionTransformer, L206, is a compact 35 lines. Patchification is a single nn.Conv2d whose kernel size equals its stride equals the patch size (conv1, L211) — for ViT-B/32 that chops a 224-pixel image into a 7-by-7 grid of 32-pixel patches. Its forward, L223 reshapes the grid into a token sequence, prepends the class embedding, adds learned positional embeddings, runs the stack, then takes only the class-token position, applies a post LayerNorm, and matmuls with the proj matrix into the joint space.

Two details in the building blocks reward attention. QuickGELU, L166 is x * sigmoid(1.702 * x) — not the exact GELU, but close enough at speed, and frozen into the checkpoints now, so any reimplementation must match it bit-for-bit to reproduce logits (our consistency test below enforces exactly that). And LayerNorm, L157 is a subclass that upcasts to float32 and back, a pragmatic fix for fp16 instability that the weight-conversion helper, L375 relies on when it halves all conv, linear, and attention weights at load time.

The ResNet branch is equally opinionated. ModifiedResNet, L94 replaces the usual 7x7 stride-2 stem with three 3x3 convolutions and swaps every strided convolution for an average-pool-then-convolve pair to reduce aliasing. Its head is not average pooling at all but AttentionPool2d, L58, a single-query multi-head attention over all spatial positions whose output projection lands directly in the joint embedding width.

The text tower reuses the same Transformer, L195 class, this time with a causal mask built by build_attention_mask, L328 — a plain upper-triangular tensor filled with negative infinity. encode_text, L343 then does something charmingly low-tech to pool the sequence: since the end-of-text token has the highest vocabulary id, text.argmax(dim=-1) locates the true end of every (padded) caption, and that position’s hidden state is projected into the joint space.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s install line still works verbatim:

pip install ftfy regex tqdm
pip install git+https://github.com/openai/CLIP.git

setup.py is a bare-bones packaging of the clip package, with include_package_data=True plus a one-line MANIFEST.in ensuring the 1.3 MB vocabulary gzip rides along in the wheel. The minimal round trip uses only APIs verified in the checked-out source:

import torch, clip
from PIL import Image

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
model, preprocess = clip.load("ViT-B/32", device=device)

image = preprocess(Image.open("pic.jpg")).unsqueeze(0).to(device)
text = clip.tokenize(["a photo of a cat", "a photo of a dog"]).to(device)

with torch.no_grad():
    image_features = model.encode_image(image)
    text_features = model.encode_text(text)

    logits_per_image, logits_per_text = model(image, text)
    probs = logits_per_image.softmax(dim=-1).cpu().numpy()
print(probs)

Under the hood, load, L94 downloads the checkpoint into ~/.cache/clip, trusting the SHA-256 embedded in the URL — _download, L43 re-downloads with a warning if the local file’s hash drifts. It first tries torch.jit.load; on failure it falls back to a state dict and rebuilds the eager module via build_model. On CPU it forces float32. The returned preprocess comes from _transform, L79: resize and center-crop to the model’s native resolution with bicubic interpolation, convert to RGB, and normalize with the exact web-crawl statistics baked into the training run — (0.48145466, 0.4578275, 0.40821073) mean and (0.26862954, 0.26130258, 0.27577711) std, numbers you will meet in dozens of downstream repos. tokenize, L205 returns a padded int tensor of shape [batch, 77] and raises rather than silently truncating unless you pass truncate=True.

The Tokenizer: One Gzip File Is the Whole Vocabulary

clip/simple_tokenizer.py is 132 lines, and its universe of symbols is bpe_simple_vocab_16e6.txt.gz — a vocabulary learned over roughly 16.6 million text pairs. SimpleTokenizer.__init__, L62 unpacks the gzip, skips the first version line, and keeps the merge table slice merges[1:49152-256-2+1] — 48,894 learned merges. Add the 256 reversible byte characters from bytes_to_unicode, L16 (the GPT-2 trick of remapping raw bytes onto printable unicode so BPE never emits UNKs), the same 256 with an end-of-word marker, and two special tokens, and the encoder lands at exactly 49,408 entries — the vocab_size every checkpoint reports.

Encoding is equally transparent. encode, L121 runs basic_clean, L50 (ftfy plus a double HTML unescape), then whitespace_clean, L56, lowercases, and splits with a case-insensitive regex that keeps contractions, letter runs, single digits, and punctuation runs apart. Each fragment is byte-mapped and greedily merged by bpe, L80, which repeatedly applies the lowest-ranked adjacent pair and caches results per token. decode, L129 inverts the mapping and turns end-of-word markers back into spaces. That is the contrast with industrial tokenizers: no configurability, no non-Latin handling — just the frozen artifact the model was trained against.

Zero-Shot Classification, Verified by One Test

Because the CI workflow pins Python 3.8 against PyTorch 1.7.1, 1.9.1 and 1.10.1, the repository’s only test has to be robust across three generations of the framework. It parametrizes over all nine model names, loads each checkpoint twice — once with jit=True, once eager — runs the CLIP.png figure through both, and asserts the softmax probabilities agree within atol=0.01, rtol=0.1. That is precisely the failure mode QuickGELU and the LayerNorm cast would cause if a reimplementation drifted.

For an end-to-end zero-shot loop, the README’s CIFAR-100 example remains the canonical template: encode one image, encode one caption per class (optionally averaging over prompt templates), softmax, sort. The Interacting with CLIP notebook walks the same path interactively, including probability inspection per prompt. Everything you might bolt on afterwards — embedding caches, image search, or the ONNX export we covered in our /onnx/ tour — consumes exactly the two encode_* methods.

Honest Limits

The repository is a frozen research artifact, and the authors say so in model-card.md: the models are “intended as a research output,” any deployed use is out of scope, and the training code and 400-million-pair dataset were never released. You get checkpoints and inference scaffolding, nothing more. The code also shows its age — it warns below PyTorch 1.7.1, and the JIT path reaches into torch-internal graph nodes to patch device constants.

The tokenizer is English-only by construction: the 49,408-entry BPE table was learned from English web text, and the model card restricts use to English prompts — multilingual successors like SigLIP had to rebuild both towers and vocabularies from scratch. Prompt phrasing is a real sensitivity, not a footnote: the paper’s own Table 9 ablations show large swings from template choices, which is why the exact templates ship as data. Resolution is capped by the checkpoint — input_resolution is read from the state dict, 224 pixels for the standard ViTs (a 7x7 patch grid at patch size 32) with 336 available only as the separate ViT-L/14@336px checkpoint — so fine detail below the patch size is simply unreachable. And the 77-token context is a hard ceiling: tokenize either raises or silently replaces the tail of long captions with the end-of-text token, and since pooling reads exactly that end-of-text position, anything truncated is information the text tower never sees. Finally, treat the similarity outputs as logits-to-be-tempered, not probabilities: the learned logit_scale was fit during contrastive training, so raw cosine thresholds will not transfer across models or domains.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of OpenAI CLIP: contrastive language-image pretraining, the ViT and text transformer dual encoder, the 49,408-entry BPE tokenizer, and zero-shot classification.

entry.title: open_clip: A Source Tour of the Maintained Open CLIP Implementation

link.title: open_clip: A Source Tour of the Maintained Open CLIP Implementation

entry.content:
When OpenAI released CLIP in 2021 it changed how the community thinks about vision-language pretraining: two towers, a temperature-scaled contrastive objective, and zero-shot classification from prompt templates. The original repository — which we walked through in the earlier tour of /clip/ — shipped the weights and a minimal inference API, but training was never its focus. Its code froze shortly after release, and anyone who wanted to retrain, fine-tune, or extend CLIP had to start over. That gap is exactly what mlfoundations/open_clip fills. Begun as a community reimplementation of the contrastive objective, it has grown into the de facto maintained implementation: hundreds of pretrained checkpoints, native support for the SigLIP, CoCa, CLAP and MaMMUT model families, timm and HuggingFace backbones behind one factory function, and a full training package that scales from a single GPU to a multi-node cluster.

The library is deliberately thin. It is pure Python on top of PyTorch — no compiled extensions, no Cython to build, nothing to fight with on Windows or ARM — and it leans on two ecosystem workhorses that most projects already trust: timm for vision backbones and transformers for text encoders, the same library behind /transformers/. That combination is the quiet design decision that makes open_clip feel bigger than it is. A ViT-B-32 config is a handful of JSON keys; a ConvNeXt or EVA vision tower is borrowed from timm at instantiation time; a multilingual XLM-R text tower is borrowed from transformers the same way. The library adds contrastive glue, checkpoint conversion, and a registry, not another modeling framework.

This post is a source tour, in the same style as our previous posts. We start at the function every user touches first — the model factory — then descend into the pretrained-weight registry, the tokenizer bridge, and the distributed training and zero-shot evaluation flow. Two dependency graphs drawn from the actual repository structure anchor the narrative: an overview of the whole system and a detail view of how the pieces call each other.

Overview of open_clip: the training entry wires the factory, the weight registry, the tokenizer bridge, the dual-tower models, and the train/eval flow into one call graph.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L62 — the CLI entry that parses arguments, initializes the distributed device, creates the model and data, and drives the epoch loop.
  • create_model_and_transforms, L1251 — the one-stop factory returning a model plus paired training and validation preprocess transforms.
  • _PRETRAINED, L460 — the curated weight registry mapping every model and tag to a checkpoint URL or HuggingFace repo.
  • CLIP, L412 — the canonical dual-tower model with encode_image / encode_text and a learnable logit_scale.
  • VisionTransformer, L550 — the native ViT image tower; the same file hosts the causal-masked text tower and attention blocks.
  • HFTokenizer, L625 — the HuggingFace AutoTokenizer bridge that adapts arbitrary tokenizers to CLIP conventions.
  • TimmModel, L25 — the adapter that turns any timm classification backbone into a vision tower.
  • train_one_epoch, L296 — the autocast step loop with gradient accumulation, loss reduction, and metric logging.
  • build_zero_shot_classifier, L22 — builds class embeddings from prompt templates for end-of-epoch evaluation.

The Factory: One Entry Point, Many Model Families

Everything in open_clip funnels through create_model_and_transforms in src/open_clip/factory.py. It delegates to create_model, L326, which first parses the model identifier. A bare name like ViT-B-32 is looked up in the built-in configs under src/open_clip/model_configs/ — roughly 150 JSON files, each describing embed_dim, vision_cfg, and text_cfg. A prefixed name like hf-hub:org/repo instead fetches an open_clip_config.json from the HuggingFace Hub, and local-dir: reads the same format from disk. Three input styles, one config schema.

Class selection is the interesting part. Rather than hard-coding class names, the factory calls traits_from_config, L144 to classify the config into a ModelFamily, then picks the implementation: plain CLIP for the classic flat layout, CustomTextCLIP (L613) when the text tower should stay a nested module — required for HF-backed, “modern”, or variable-length text towers — plus CoCa, CLAP, MaMMUT, and the generative NaFlex classes. Once instantiated, the model exposes the familiar encode_image, L488 and encode_text, L508 methods, both with an optional normalize flag.

Weight loading is its own sub-flow. load_checkpoint, L255 accepts .safetensors files through the safetensors reader and everything else through torch.load with weights_only=True by default. Before the state dict reaches the model it is massaged: third-party checkpoints are remapped by convert_state_dict, L278, legacy flat-layout checkpoints are re-keyed into the custom-text format, logit-scale shapes are reconciled, and vision or text position embeddings are interpolated if the checkpoint’s grid size differs from the requested one. This is where years of ecosystem drift get absorbed so that a 2021 OpenAI checkpoint and a 2026 community checkpoint both load through the same call.

The Pretrained-Weight Registry

The registry in src/open_clip/pretrained.py is what makes tags like openai, laion2b_s34b_b79k, or datacomp_xl_s13b_b90k mean anything. _PRETRAINED, L460 is a large dictionary keyed by architecture, where each value maps tags to config dicts built by helpers such as _pcfg for OpenAI-style defaults. Crucially, the config carries more than a URL: it records the normalization mean/std, the resize mode, the interpolation, and a quick_gelu flag, because the original OpenAI models were trained with the QuickGELU activation and silently degrade if you run them with vanilla GELU. When a tag’s activation setting disagrees with the requested architecture variant, the factory emits a QuickGELU mismatch warning rather than letting accuracy evaporate quietly.

Lookup and download are separated cleanly. get_pretrained_cfg, L806 answers “what are the settings for this tag”, while download_pretrained, L922 resolves the checkpoint to a cached file, preferring GitHub release URLs or HuggingFace Hub downloads (download_pretrained_from_hf at L885). Over the project’s life most weights have been mirrored from GitHub releases to timm/* and laion/* Hub repos, which matters because release assets lack CDN-grade bandwidth. Several newer checkpoints ship as safetensors — the format we covered in /safetensors/ — which the loader detects by file extension and reads without pickle deserialization. For pure inference there is a shortcut, create_model_from_pretrained, that fuses model creation and transform construction in one call.

Tokenizers: the HuggingFace Bridge

The original CLIP used a bespoke byte-pair encoder trained on its caption corpus. open_clip keeps that exact implementation as SimpleTokenizer, L264, complete with the bundled BPE vocabulary, so OpenAI checkpoints tokenize identically here and in the original library. Everything newer, though, rides on HFTokenizer, L625, a wrapper around AutoTokenizer — the same dispatch layer we described in /tokenizers/. The wrapper does three things that look small and are not: it forces right-side padding so CLIP’s eos-pooling math stays correct for decoder-family tokenizers that default to left padding, it maps bos/eos/cls/sep ids into the sot/eot vocabulary the towers expect, and it applies a configurable text-cleaning chain before encoding.

Selection happens in get_tokenizer, L850: the model’s text_cfg decides between the HF bridge, the SigLIP sentencepiece tokenizer (SigLipTokenizer, L896 with Gemma, C4, or multilingual variants), a tiktoken-based tokenizer for the generative models, or the original BPE. The same text_cfg also declares context_length — 77 for classic CLIP, much longer for SigLIP and modern variants — and the factory cross-checks pad and eos ids against the pooling mode so a generative model cannot silently train with the wrong ignore index. The lesson from reading this file is that “just tokenize it” hides most of the compatibility surface in multimodal systems.

From Install to Your First Model

The package installs from PyPI under its distribution name open_clip_torch:

pip install open_clip_torch
# training extras (webdataset, pandas, transformers):
pip install "open_clip_torch[training]"

Then the full factory round-trip in a few lines:

import torch
from PIL import Image
import open_clip

model, _, preprocess = open_clip.create_model_and_transforms(
    "ViT-B-32", pretrained="laion2b_s34b_b79k"
)
tokenizer = open_clip.get_tokenizer("ViT-B-32")

image = preprocess(Image.open("dog.jpg")).unsqueeze(0)
text = tokenizer(["a diagram", "a dog", "a cat"])

with torch.no_grad(), torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.float16):
    image_features = model.encode_image(image)
    text_features = model.encode_text(text)
    image_features /= image_features.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    text_features /= text_features.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    text_probs = (100.0 * image_features @ text_features.T).softmax(dim=-1)

print(text_probs)  # per-class probabilities

Note what you did not do: no manual config parsing, no weight conversion, no activation-function bookkeeping — the tag carried all of it. Every API used above (create_model_and_transforms, get_tokenizer, encode_image, encode_text, the laion2b_s34b_b79k tag) exists verbatim in the current source tree, and the returned preprocess object is built by image_transform_v2, L501 from torchvision primitives on the mean/std the registry recorded for that tag.

Training, Distributed by Default

The open_clip_train package is where “reproduction” stops being a claim and becomes a script. main, L62 enables tf32, calls init_distributed_device, L80 — which reads torchrun’s LOCAL_RANK/RANK/WORLD_SIZE environment variables or SLURM’s equivalents, initializes torch.distributed with nccl, gloo, or hccl, and pins the device to the local rank — then assembles data with get_data, L1203, the optimizer with create_optimizer, L336 (weight-decay exclusions for norms, biases, and the logit scale, plus optional layer-wise decay), and the schedule with cosine_lr, L74. Precision is centralized in get_autocast, L6: one flag selects amp fp16, pure fp16, bf16, or fp32, and the loop picks the matching input dtype and gradient scaler.

The step loop in train_one_epoch is honest engineering rather than magic. Each batch flows through the task object — the TrainingTask contract (L30) with CLIPTask (L9) as the contrastive implementation — whose forward returns a dict of losses computed by ClipLoss, L57, a symmetric cross-entropy over the scaled image-text similarity matrix. The SigLIP objective swaps it for the pairwise sigmoid SigLipLoss, L375, and distillation and CoCa variants subclass the same base. Because open_clip is pure PyTorch underneath, every collective here is a plain dist.all_reduce — the native code path we touched on in /pytorch/ — so nothing exotic hides inside the C extensions; there are none. An --local-loss option slices the contrastive matrix per rank to save memory, and evaluation runs after each epoch through the zero-shot classifiers built from OPENAI_IMAGENET_TEMPLATES, L2, the same 80 prompts the original paper used.

Detail view: CLI and IO, the factory and its weight plumbing, the model families, tokenizer and preprocess builders, the task abstraction, the training loop, and the zero-shot eval chain.

Honest Limits

No tour is complete without the trade-offs. First, pretrained-weight licensing varies dramatically across the registry: the OpenAI originals, LAION-2B, DataComp, SigLIP, and MetaCLIP checkpoints come with different licenses and different dataset provenance, and open_clip deliberately does not normalize that away — you are expected to check the tag’s source repo before deploying. Second, checkpoint size management is on you. Registry entries now span 150 MB RN50s to multi-gigabyte ViT-bigG and EVA models; the library caches whatever you download, offers no deduplication or sharding, and load_checkpoint will happily keep both the flat and custom-text copies of a state dict in memory during conversion. Plan disk and RAM accordingly.

Third, training-data dependence is structural. CLIP-family models inherit the curation, biases, and coverage of their caption corpora — a DataComp-tuned ViT-B-32 and a LAION-tuned one of the same architecture are not interchangeable, and zero-shot gaps on underrepresented classes trace directly to what the contrastive objective saw. Fourth, tokenizer differences matter more than users expect: the original CLIP BPE, HF tokenizers, sentencepiece SigLIP variants, and tiktoken-based generative tokenizers are not drop-in swappable, text embeddings are not portable across checkpoints with different vocabularies, and the classic 77-token context length is an architectural constraint, not a soft default. Finally, quickGELU and preprocessing mismatches are silent until you evaluate — the warnings exist, but only comparison against published numbers will catch a subtle preprocessing drift. Treat the registry’s mean/std/interpolation fields as part of the model definition, because that is how the source treats them.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of mlfoundations/open_clip: the model factory, the pretrained-weight registry, the HuggingFace tokenizer bridge, and the distributed training flow with zero-shot evaluation.

entry.title: Inside TensorFlow 2: Eager Execution, tf.function Tracing, and the Grappler Machine

link.title: Inside TensorFlow 2: Eager Execution, tf.function Tracing, and the Grappler Machine

entry.content:
TensorFlow has a strange reputation problem. Ten years ago it was the framework everyone complained about: graphs, sessions, feed dictionaries, a learning curve shaped like a wall. TensorFlow 2 deleted almost all of that. There is no tf.Session anymore, no placeholder, no manual graph building. You write ordinary Python, ops run immediately, results come back as tensors you can print(). And yet the graph machinery never went away — it just moved underneath you, so well hidden that most users never meet it.

That hidden machinery is what this post tours. We will read the actual source of the TensorFlow repository, branch master, and follow two execution paths that every training step takes. The first is the eager path: what literally happens between tf.add(a, b) and a number on your screen. The second is the traced path: what happens when you slap @tf.function on that same code, where the Python body is re-executed in a special graph-capturing mode, and where the legendary Grappler optimizer gets its chance to rewrite everything before a single kernel runs. If you know Keras, you have used the top of this stack; here we go three layers below it. And if you have read our tours of JAX or PyTorch, you will notice the same evolutionary pressure at work: everyone converged on “eager first, trace later.”

The overview below is the whole story in one picture. The left groups are Python, the middle is the C boundary, the right is the C++ runtime plus Grappler, the graph optimizer that runs whenever a traced function is defined.

TensorFlow 2 runtime: Python front-end, the tf.function tracing layer, the TFE C boundary, the C++ eager executor, and Grappler feeding optimized FunctionDefs back into execution.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • tf.function, L1319 — the decorator you actually call; it wraps your Python callable in a Function object with a per-signature cache.
  • _maybe_define_function, L188 — on every call, computes a cache key and decides whether to trace a new concrete function or reuse an existing one.
  • FuncGraph, L134 — a subclass of ops.Graph that records every op your Python body executes while “taping” the run.
  • quick_execute, L28 — the pybind entry point for single eager ops; execute = quick_execute is literally an alias at line 131.
  • TFE_Execute, L924 — the C API call that crosses the Python/C++ boundary.
  • EagerOperation::Reset, L330 — builds the mutable op object: name, attrs, inputs, device.
  • EagerExecutor::AddOrExecute, L135 — runs the node synchronously in eager mode or queues it when async execution is enabled.
  • KernelAndDeviceFunc::Run, L437 — the final hop: invoke the FunctionLibraryRuntime and registered kernels on a device.
  • MetaOptimizer::OptimizeGraph, L782 — Grappler’s scheduler, which runs a fixed roster of graph rewriting passes.

Eager by Default: Anatomy of a Single Op

In TF1, an op call appended a node to a graph and did nothing else. In TF2, tf.add(a, b) computes. The generated Python wrapper eventually lands in execute.py, whose quick_execute receives the op name, inputs, attrs, and the global Context, L519 — the process-wide object that knows whether you are in eager mode, which devices exist, and how tensors are placed. From there the call crosses into C++ through TFE_Execute, where an EagerOperation is reset and filled with the op’s metadata, then handed to the executor.

The executor is where TensorFlow’s async mode lives. By default, EagerExecutor::SyncExecute runs the node on the calling thread and blocks. If you enable async execution, AddOrExecute enqueues the node and returns immediately — the op appears to have completed, but the actual kernel launch happens on a background thread, and errors surface later, when you touch the output. This is the same trick PyTorch plays with its CUDA streams: keep the Python thread responsive, let the device lag behind.

At the bottom of the eager path sits KernelAndDeviceOp::Run in kernel_and_device.cc, L287, which resolves the op’s registered kernel for the target device and launches it. Outputs come back wrapped as TensorHandles — lazy references that may or may not yet contain computed data. Every eager object you see in Python, including the EagerTensor you print, is a thin Python skin over one of these handles.

tf.function: Tracing, Caches, and Concrete Functions

The eager path is convenient but slow per-op: every call pays Python dispatch, attribute validation, and a C boundary crossing. tf.function is the escape hatch. When you call a decorated function, Function.__call__ at polymorphic_function.py, L809 consults a cache keyed on argument types and shapes. A miss triggers _maybe_define_function in tracing_compilation.py, L188, which is where the interesting transformation happens.

Tracing re-executes your Python body, but inside a FuncGraph. Tensors flowing through the graph are placeholders; every TensorFlow op you call is appended to the FuncGraph instead of executing. Python control flow is unrolled at trace time — an if on a tensor value either works via AutoGraph’s rewriting or just takes one branch forever, which is the single most common source of tf.function bugs. The captured graph is then packaged by from_func_graph at atomic_function.py, L471 into an AtomicFunction, a lean executable wrapper, and stored in a ConcreteFunction (concrete_function.py, L1019) pinned to one input signature.

This design explains the behavior everyone learns the hard way: call your function with a [None, 784] tensor and a [32, 784] tensor and you get two traces, two graphs, two copies of your weights’ references. Pin shapes with input_signature and the cache stays small. When you suspect tracing trouble, tf.config.run_functions_eagerly(True) — implemented in eager_function_run.py, L32 — flips every function back to plain eager execution, which is usually enough to isolate the bug. The trace-then-cache pattern should be familiar from JAX: both frameworks bet that the first call is expensive and every later call should be pure C++.

Grappler: The Optimizer That Runs Before You Notice

Here is the part of TF2 that has no PyTorch equivalent. The moment a FuncGraph is finalized, it can be handed to Grappler, TensorFlow’s graph optimizer. The item builder at grappler_item_builder.cc, L296 wraps the GraphDef together with its fetch tensors and init ops into a GrapplerItem, and MetaOptimizer::OptimizeGraph runs the passes in a fixed schedule: constant folding, arithmetic simplification, op fusion, function inlining, layout optimization, and more, each implemented as a self-contained rewriter.

Constant folding (constant_folding.cc, L4057) precomputes subgraphs whose inputs are all known. The arithmetic optimizer (arithmetic_optimizer.cc, L4489) removes redundant multiplications and reassociates the data flow so that common patterns collapse. Remapper (remapper.cc, L5021) fuses Conv2D with BatchNorm and activations into single kernels — a direct speedup for every CNN trained through Keras. The function optimizer (function_optimizer.cc, L1528) works on the function library itself, inlining and specializing FunctionDefs. Several passes lean on static shape inference from GraphProperties, L2538, and when the meta-optimizer needs a real device to measure against, SingleMachine::Initialize, L142 provisions a local cluster for the job.

The result is that a @tf.function you wrote naively often runs significantly faster than the same code run eagerly, before you touch XLA at all. Other stacks expose similar machinery — ONNX Runtime and TVM both do graph-level rewrites — but Grappler’s framing is unusual: it is always on, mostly invisible, and tuned more for training graphs than for deployment-time minification.

From Install to Your First Model

The install is the boring part:

pip install tensorflow

Now a minimal snippet that deliberately walks both paths from the diagrams — an eager function, a traced function with a pinned signature, and the eager-mode debug switch:

import tensorflow as tf

def dense(x, w, b):
    return tf.add(tf.matmul(x, w), b)

w = tf.Variable(tf.random.normal([784, 32]))
b = tf.Variable(tf.zeros([32]))

# Eager path: each call goes quick_execute -> TFE_Execute -> kernels.
y1 = dense(tf.ones([1, 784]), w, b)

# Traced path: first call traces a FuncGraph, later calls reuse it.
fast = tf.function(dense, input_signature=[
    tf.TensorSpec([None, 784], tf.float32), w, b])
y2 = fast(tf.ones([1, 784]))   # trace happens here
y3 = fast(tf.ones([5, 784]))   # cache hit: same concrete function

# Debug: pretend it is 2026 but execute like 2020-eager.
tf.config.run_functions_eagerly(True)
y4 = fast(tf.ones([2, 784]))   # no tracing, pure eager again
tf.config.run_functions_eagerly(False)

Three calls, three different stories: y1 crosses the C boundary twice per op, every time. y2 and y3 hit the same cached concrete function — the None in the signature means both batch sizes share one trace. y4 skips the cache entirely. Add print(w.shape) after any of these and you are back to ordinary Python debugging.

Honest Limits

Binary size is enormous. The CPU-only pip wheel approaches 600 MB installed, and with CUDA libraries the footprint grows by gigabytes. Compare llama.cpp or GGML, which run models from a single binary. TensorFlow’s runtime carries ten years of op registry, Grappler passes, and kernel implementations for every device it might meet.

Graph-mode complexity did not disappear; it moved. The session is gone, but retracing surprises, AutoGraph edge cases, and the “Python side effects run only at trace time” rule are all still there, now documented in caveats rather than fixed by design. Teams shipping large tf.function codebases still maintain shape-signature discipline by hand.

XLA compile latency is real. tf.function(jit_compile=True) can transform performance on TPU and GPU, but the first call pays a full compile, and dynamic shapes force recompilation. For latency-sensitive serving, this trade needs the same budgeting you would give any ahead-of-time compiler.

Windows is a second-class platform. Since release 2.11, native Windows pip packages are CPU-only; GPU support requires WSL2. Linux remains the target the build system actually optimizes for, and CI behavior reflects it.

Export is graph-shaped. SavedModel serializes concrete functions, which means deployment tooling inherits the traced view of your model — one more reason the tracing internals above matter even if you never read them in anger. When the target is a leaner runtime, exporting to ONNX and serving with specialized runtimes remains the pragmatic route.

Where TensorFlow Sits in the Stack

TensorFlow today is a full-stack compiler wearing a Python API as a mask: eager mode for development speed, tracing for execution efficiency, Grappler for free wins, XLA for the last mile. The layers are genuinely separable — Keras users live entirely above them, JAX proved you can expose only the traced layer and still win, and the serving ecosystem downstream (vLLM, TGI) mostly consumes the exported graph form. Reading the source makes the whole stack feel less like magic: it is one long chain from def function(...) to a kernel launch, with a very determined optimizer standing guard in the middle.
entry.summary: A source tour of TensorFlow's session-less runtime: how eager ops execute through the TFE C API, how tf.function traces and caches concrete functions, and how Grappler optimizes the graph before it runs.

entry.title: torchaudio Source Tour: TorchCodec I/O, Custom Autograd, and the C++/CUDA Kernels Behind Forced Alignment

link.title: torchaudio Source Tour: TorchCodec I/O, Custom Autograd, and the C++/CUDA Kernels Behind Forced Alignment

entry.content:
Most people meet torchaudio as a one-liner: torchaudio.load("clip.wav") returns a tensor and a sample rate, and that is the end of the story. Under the hood, though, the pytorch/audio repository is a fascinating case study in how a PyTorch domain library evolves. It is a smaller sibling to PyTorch itself — same extension philosophy, same tensor-first design — but it has just gone through the most radical simplification of any PyTorch-ecosystem project: the entire decoding stack was ripped out and replaced by a delegation to TorchCodec, while the hand-written CPU and CUDA kernels that actually do the hard math stayed put in a C++ library called libtorchaudio.

That combination makes the current main branch unusually readable. There is no more backend-selection maze for sox versus soundfile versus ffmpeg; load and save now forward to TorchCodec’s AudioDecoder and AudioEncoder. Meanwhile, performance-critical code — Viterbi-style forced alignment, RNN-transducer loss, CUDA IIR filtering — still lives in C++ and CUDA files, registered as custom torch ops through the new stable library ABI. If you enjoyed the image-side twin of this story in torchvision, you will recognize the pattern: a thin Python surface, a compact C++ extension, and everything else expressed as composable tensor ops.

This post walks the tree the way an engineer would: the Python entry points first, the extension-loading mechanics second, then the native kernels, and finally the honest trade-offs — because a library in maintenance mode deserves an honest map, not a brochure.

Overview of torchaudio on the main branch: the Python surface delegates I/O to TorchCodec, boots native extensions at import time, and routes specialized math into libtorchaudio's CPU/CUDA kernels.

The overview rewards a slow read. Reading the overview from left to right:

  • load, L18 — the public entry point. Its docstring now says plainly: as of TorchAudio 2.9 this relies on TorchCodec’s decoding under the hood.
  • load_with_torchcodec, L9 — the actual implementation, which builds a TorchCodec AudioDecoder, fetches metadata, and returns float32 samples.
  • _load_lib("_torchaudio"), L30 — import-time initialization that loads the extension modules before anything else runs.
  • torch.ops.load_library, L56 — the glob-based loader that finds .so (or .pyd on Windows) binaries and registers their ops.
  • MelSpectrogram, L515 — the nn.Module wrapper layer, where every transform stays composable and TorchScript-friendly.
  • lfilter, L1032 — an IIR filter implemented with custom autograd, dispatching into native code.
  • STABLE_TORCH_LIBRARY_FRAGMENT, L118 — the C++ side that declares the _lfilter_core_loop op and binds CPU, CUDA, and composite-fallback implementations.
  • torch.ops.torchaudio.forced_align, L72 — the call that jumps from pure Python straight into the compiled alignment kernel.
  • falign_cuda_step_kernel, L26 — the CUDA kernel that performs the alignment sweep on GPU.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is deliberately boring, because TorchAudio 2.11 rides along with any modern torch build instead of pinning one:

pip install torchaudio

Note that load and save now require torchcodec to be importable (it ships in the CUDA and standard wheels; on some platforms you install it separately). Once it is there, the round trip works exactly as it always did:

import torch, torchaudio

waveform, sr = torchaudio.load("speech.wav")          # [channel, time] float32
waveform_16k = torchaudio.functional.resample(waveform, sr, 16000)

torchaudio.save("speech_16k.wav", waveform_16k, 16000)

mel = torchaudio.transforms.MelSpectrogram(
    sample_rate=16000, n_fft=1024, hop_length=256
)(waveform_16k)
print(mel.shape)   # e.g. torch.Size([1, 64, T])

Every call in that snippet was verified against the checked-out source: resample lives in the functional layer, and MelSpectrogram composes spectrogram plus a mel filterbank without ever leaving tensor land, which is exactly what makes it exportable to other runtimes such as Executorch for on-device audio.

One Call Away From the Metal: the lfilter Dispatch Chain

lfilter is the best place to watch the Python-to-C++ chain in this library. On the Python side, filtering.py pads the waveform, flips the coefficient tensors, and then calls an opaque op named _lfilter_core_loop. Three things make this more interesting than a plain loop:

  1. Custom autograd. DifferentiableIIR (at L983) and its FIR sibling define forward/backward pairs, so filtering an audio batch is trainable end to end — you can put a biquad before a loss and let gradients flow through the recurrence.
  2. Multi-backend dispatch. In lfilter.cpp, one op schema gets three bindings: a CPU implementation, a CUDA implementation, and a CompositeExplicitAutograd fallback for anything else. The CUDA branch is implemented in iir_cuda.cu, whose iir_cu_kernel (at L11) parallelizes across batch and channel while walking time sequentially — the classic IIR compromise.
  3. The stable library ABI. These files use STABLE_TORCH_LIBRARY_FRAGMENT and TORCH_BOX rather than the older C++ extension API. That is the same direction the rest of the PyTorch ecosystem is taking: register ops by schema string, keep ABI churn out of downstream builds.

The same pattern repeats for the effects that came over from sox heritage: overdrive, L1150 on the Python side has its kernel twin in overdrive.cpp, registered under _overdrive_core_loop. The biquad family (lowpass_biquad, equalizer_biquad, bass_biquad, and friends) stays in pure torch and only reuses the lfilter machinery — a nice example of paying the native-code toll only where the recurrence demands it.

Forced Alignment and Transducer Loss, Compiled

The crown jewels of libtorchaudio are the sequence models’ kernels. Forced alignment — aligning a known transcript to audio emissions, CTC-style — is a dynamic-programming scan that Python would crawl through. The flow here is textbook clean:

  • The Python wrapper forced_align, L12 validates shapes, fills default lengths, guards itself with fail_if_no_align (a decorator built from fail_with_message, L61), then calls the op.
  • The op signature is declared in compute.cpp, L4 — five arguments in, paths and scores out.
  • Two implementations exist: the CPU scan in forced_align_impl, L19, and the GPU sweep in falign_cuda_step_kernel, L26. Both feed results back as label-per-timestep tensors that merge_tokens collapses into TokenSpan, L77 objects.

RNN-transducer loss follows the same shape but with heavier machinery. The Python rnnt_loss (at L1747) calls torch.ops.torchaudio.rnnt_loss_forward, L1725; the schema in rnnt/compute.cpp, L4 accepts a clamp value and a fused_log_softmax flag; and the CUDA implementation drives a workspace-based GpuTransducer whose alpha/beta scans are split into separate cooperative kernels. There is even a third decoding path: the cuctc subfolder ships a CUDA prefix-scoring CTC decoder whose ops are registered in python_binding.cpp, L113 and driven by CUCTCDecoder, L42. These kernels pair naturally with the reference RNNT, L453 model, which composes an Emformer encoder with a transducer head — and they complement generic serving stacks like TorchServe when you need aligned, token-level outputs rather than plain logits.

The Functional Layer and Transform Wrappers

Everything that does not need custom C++ stays in two pure-torch files, and that is most of the library. functional.py opens with spectrogram (at L54), then provides griffinlim, melscale_fbanks (at L518), phase-based pitch_shift, fftconvolve, beamforming utilities, and masking helpers for SpecAugment-style training. The _transforms.py file wraps these as nn.Modules — Resample (at L908) caches its kernel, SpecAugment (at L1290) composes the two masking ops, and RNNTLoss (at L1792) puts the native loss behind a module call so it slots into ordinary training loops. The split is a good design template: functions are stateless math, modules own configuration and cached state, and native ops are invoked only at the innermost, hot level.

Two more corners of the Python tree are worth knowing about. The compliance package reproduces Kaldi’s feature extractors (compliance.kaldi.fbank, mfcc) bit-for-bit, which sounds academic until you have to drop a checkpoint trained in an old speech stack into a torch training loop and get identical features. And the datasets and models packages carry the reference implementations — WaveRNN, Tacotron2, DeepSpeech, ConvTasNet — kept not as a model zoo to download from, but as executable documentation for how these architectures compose with the transforms above. Reading conv_tasnet.py next to functional.py teaches mask-based source separation in about four hundred lines.

Honest Limits

This is a library in maintenance mode, and the README says so directly: features were deprecated from TorchAudio 2.8 and removed in 2.9, with the goal of scoping the project to “processing audio data for ML”. Concretely, what you give up and what you should watch for:

  • The backend matrix is gone. Releases up to 2.8 offered three interchangeable I/O backends with real platform asymmetries: the sox backend was never shipped in Windows wheels, soundfile worked everywhere but could not stream or apply effects, and the ffmpeg backend dlopened versioned shared libraries with an ABI range per release. On main, all of that is replaced by TorchCodec, which is FFmpeg-based — so FFmpeg is still the true dependency, just one layer down and managed by another project. Check TorchCodec’s own platform matrix before betting a deployment on it.
  • Compatibility parameters are accepted and ignored. load still takes normalize, buffer_size, and backend, but they do nothing except emit warnings (see the guard clauses at the top of load_with_torchcodec). Output is always normalized float32; normalize=False will not give you int16 samples anymore.
  • Whole-file decode, then slice. Offset handling is post-hoc: the decoder fetches everything (get_all_samples, L128) and only afterwards applies frame_offset/num_frames slicing. For a three-hour audiobook, loading thirty seconds still decodes the whole file into memory first. The docstring points you at torchcodec.decoders.AudioDecoder directly for time-based seeking when that matters.
  • Strict native-version checks. _check_cuda_version, L116 raises at import time if torch and torchaudio were built against different CUDA majors, and the Windows loader needs the old conda-PATH workaround (_init_dll_path, L101) plus .pyd globbing — reminders that native wheels still bite hardest on Windows.
  • Alignment constraints. forced_align refuses batches larger than one (the check lives in the CPU impl: “The batch dimension for targets must be 1”, L177), forbids blank tokens in targets, and requires the alignment extension to have been compiled in at all — the availability flag is probed via is_align_available, L37 rather than assumed.
  • Export, not extension. With save relying on TorchCodec’s AudioEncoder (at L157), exotic encodings and bit-depth controls that sox once offered have no equivalent; and since the library follows torch’s release train without pinning it, CI matrices that assumed one-torch-one-torchaudio need updating.

None of this diminishes the engineering here. What remains is a tight, legible core: TorchCodec for bytes-to-tensor, pure torch for the wide middle, and a small, well-guarded native layer — libtorchaudio — for the algorithms that genuinely need compiled code. For interoperability beyond torch, the tensor shapes line up nicely with ONNX export paths, and the same thin-Python-over-native-kernels philosophy shows up across the ecosystem, from serving frameworks to this very repository. Read it while it is small; maintenance-mode codebases rarely stay this approachable for long.
entry.summary: A guided tour of the pytorch/audio source tree: how torchaudio.load hands decoding to TorchCodec, how lfilter dispatches into libtorchaudio CPU/CUDA kernels, and where the maintenance-mode limits are.

entry.title: torchvision Under the Hood: transforms v2 and the C++ Ops That Power Detection

link.title: torchvision Under the Hood: transforms v2 and the C++ Ops That Power Detection

entry.content:
Most people treat torchvision as a convenience layer: a Resize here, a pretrained ResNet there. But if you train or deploy detection models, you are standing on a much more interesting machine. The torchvision.transforms.v2 package rebuilt augmentation around a single Transform base class that understands whole samples — image, masks, bounding boxes, keypoints, labels — and moves them together through every staged operation. And the torchvision.ops package hides hand-written C++ and CUDA kernels for the operations that inference servers actually burn cycles on: non-maximum suppression, RoI alignment, deformable convolution. This post walks that machine from the Python surface down to the .cu files, continuing our series of source tours where we previously went inside PyTorch itself and compared it against TensorFlow.

The two diagrams below were generated directly from the pytorch/vision repository on the main branch. The overview shows the full arc: user-facing v2 transforms on the left, the type-driven kernel dispatch in the middle, compiled ops and their CUDA kernels on the right, and the Faster R-CNN detection stack that ties both halves together.

torchvision at a glance: the v2 transform engine on the left feeds type-dispatched kernels; on the right, Python op wrappers hand off to registered C++/CUDA kernels that detection models like Faster R-CNN consume.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • transforms.v2, L1 — one flat namespace that re-exports every v2 transform, from Compose to SanitizeBoundingBoxes, so user code never has to know the internal module layout.
  • Compose, L11 — the container that chains transforms; its forward, L49 passes the entire sample tuple through each step in order.
  • Transform, L17 — the base class whose forward, L57 flattens the whole sample, samples parameters once, and transforms only the leaves that need it.
  • _get_kernel, L99 — the registry that resolves which functional kernel runs for a given input type; register_kernel, L70 is the extension point.
  • RandomResizedCrop, L201 — the workhorse of classification augmentation, part of a spatial catalog that also includes detection-specific RandomIoUCrop, L1123.
  • ColorJitter, L72 — the photometric family, plus RandomPhotometricDistort, L185, the SSD-style distorter.
  • nms, L20 — the Python face of suppression, which calls the compiled op at L54 after checking the C extension is present.
  • nms_kernel, L165 — the CUDA entry point that launches a blockwise IoU computation and gather_keep_from_mask, L104 collects the survivors.
  • RoIHeads, L504 — the second detection stage, whose postprocess_detections, L680 is a direct consumer of the ops on the right side of the diagram.

One Sample In, Everything Together

The v1 transforms API was built for a single image; the v2 API was built for a sample. The key decision lives in Transform.forward, L57: whatever you pass — a tensor, a (img, target) pair, a dict with masks and boxes — gets flattened with torch’s pytree machinery into a list of leaves plus a spec. Then _needs_transform_list decides which leaves are actually transformed. Pure tensors are passed through untouched when an explicit Image or Video is present in the sample, so the numeric labels in your detection target survive a Resize without being accidentally treated as pixels. That heuristic is documented at length in _needs_transform_list, L75, and it is the reason v2 can keep backward compatibility for bare-tensor callers while still protecting structured targets.

The sample leaves are usually tv_tensors objects: tensor subclasses that carry just enough metadata for geometry to stay correct. Image, L11 remembers that it is CHW; BoundingBoxes, L63 remembers its format (XYXY, XYWH, CXCYWH) and its canvas_size, so a crop can re-coordinatize boxes instead of silently corrupting them. When a spatial transform runs, it needs the ground truth of “how big is the image” and “where are the boxes” — helpers like get_bounding_boxes, L156 and query_size, L195 extract that from the flattened sample, and check_type, L221 implements the type matching used everywhere else.

Each subclass then overrides only two methods: make_params draws randomness once per call, and transform applies it to each flagged leaf. That split is what makes paired augmentation cheap — a flip decides its side once, then applies the same decision to image, boxes, and masks without re-rolling dice. Metadata-only transforms live in their own corner: ConvertBoundingBoxFormat, L8 and ClampBoundingBoxes, L27 mutate coordinates without touching pixels, and SanitizeBoundingBoxes, L360 drops degenerate boxes after aggressive crops — an unglamorous but essential step for detection training stability.

The Kernel Registry: Type-Driven Dispatch

A v2 transform never hardcodes “if PIL do X, if tensor do Y”. Instead, when its transform() method needs real work done, it calls self._call_kernel(functional, inpt, ...), which lands in _get_kernel, L99. The registry is keyed by the pair of functional name and input type: F.resize has one kernel for Image, another for Video, another for PIL images, and a passthrough for anything it does not recognize. The public register_kernel, L70 decorator lets third-party tensor subclasses plug into the same chain — wrap your type, register a kernel, and every built-in transform instantly works with it.

This design is why the catalog can stay small and readable. RandomResizedCrop, L201 is essentially parameter math plus a kernel call; the device- and type-specific branches live in the functional layer instead. The photometric side works the same way: ColorJitter, L72 composes brightness, contrast, saturation, and hue functionals, while RandomPhotometricDistort, L185 wraps that jitter with random channel permutation to reproduce SSD’s augmentation recipe. Even the exotic family plays along — TrivialAugmentWide, L445 and its siblings in _auto_augment.py sample an op and magnitude, then dispatch through the same registry. Mixing recipes like MixUp, L220 or JPEG, L337 (synthetic compression artifacts) round out the catalog, and ToImage, L35 plus ToDtype, L253 handle the canonical end-of-chain conversions.

NMS From Python to CUDA

Non-maximum suppression is the highest-traffic op in any detection deployment, and torchvision implements it three times: once per device that matters. The Python wrapper nms, L20 validates the extension, then dispatches through torch.ops.torchvision.nms at L54 — the same call also routes to a quantized kernel when the inputs qualify. On the C++ side, the op registration, L16 defines torchvision::nms in the stable library block at L26, and the dispatcher picks the backend.

The CPU path in nms_kernel_impl, L18 is the textbook algorithm: sort by score, walk the boxes, suppress overlaps above the IoU threshold. The CUDA path is where it gets clever. nms_kernel, L165 tiles the boxes into blocks, computes a pairwise IoU matrix in shared memory, and then gather_keep_from_mask, L104 reduces the per-block suppression bitmasks into the final keep list — turning an O(n²) serial loop into a parallel scan that stays fast even at thousands of detections. Beyond plain NMS, batched_nms, L57 offsets boxes per class index so a single suppression call handles all labels, and rotated boxes get their own compiled path through box_iou_rotated, L22. All of this is invisible to the caller, which is exactly the point: when you export a model to ONNX or serve it behind TorchServe, the same registered op name resolves on whichever device the server picked.

RoIAlign, Deformable Convolution, and the FPN Glue

Two more compiled ops carry the detection stack. RoIAlign fixes the quantization error that made older RoIPool lossy: roi_align, L204 passes sampling_ratio and aligned flags down through the registered op at L283, and the module wrapper RoIAlign, L288 makes it layer-composable. The C++ entry at Tensor roi_align, L16 fans out to a scalar CPU kernel (roi_align_forward_kernel_impl, L20) and a GPU twin (roi_align_forward_kernel_impl, L80) that assigns one CUDA thread per output bin and bilinearly samples four points.

Deformable convolution is the heavyweight: deform_conv2d, L14 forwards offsets through the op call at L92 into a C++ entry (Tensor deform_conv2d, L16) and then a trio of CUDA kernels — deformable_im2col_kernel, L162 gathers offset-sampled patches, deformable_col2im_kernel, L404 scatters input gradients, and deformable_col2im_coord_kernel, L673 computes the gradients with respect to the offsets themselves. The glue that assembles these into a model is MultiScaleRoIAlign, L230, which maps each proposal to an FPN level by area and runs RoIAlign per level. Faster R-CNN consumes all of it: FasterRCNN, L43 wires a TwoMLPHead, L286 onto the pooled features, while RoIHeads, L504 handles proposal sampling (select_training_samples, L642), the loss (fastrcnn_loss, L12), and final NMS. The in-model normalization stage, GeneralizedRCNNTransform, L86, is itself a mini version of the v2 idea — resize and normalize, but track image_sizes so box decoding stays exact.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is one line alongside PyTorch, and the CUDA wheels bundle the prebuilt ops — no local toolchain needed:

pip install torchvision

The v2 API accepts plain tensors, but it shines on structured detection samples. Everything in this snippet is a public symbol verified in the main source:

import torch
from torchvision import tv_tensors
from torchvision.transforms import v2

img = tv_tensors.Image(torch.rand(3, 256, 256))
target = {
    "boxes": tv_tensors.BoundingBoxes(
        [[20, 30, 200, 220]], format="XYXY", canvas_size=(256, 256)
    ),
    "labels": torch.tensor([7]),
}

t = v2.Compose([
    v2.RandomPhotometricDistort(p=0.5),
    v2.RandomZoomOut(fill={tv_tensors.Image: (123, 117, 104), "others": 0}),
    v2.RandomIoUCrop(),
    v2.RandomHorizontalFlip(p=0.5),
    v2.ToImage(),
    v2.ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True),
    v2.SanitizeBoundingBoxes(),
])

img_out, target_out = t(img, target)   # boxes stay valid through every step

For classification, a single v2.RandomResizedCrop(size=(224, 224), antialias=True) in the same chain covers the classic recipe. Because Compose is just an nn.Module subclass, the finished chain drops into a DataLoader worker unchanged, and the same ops run server-side if you later push the model through ExecuTorch or any runtime that links the torchvision extension.

Honest Limits

The design carries real trade-offs. First, the compiled ops are a deployment tax: torch.ops.torchvision.* symbols are only available when the C/CUDA extension is built or a matching wheel is installed, and building from source requires a full CUDA toolchain pinned to your PyTorch version. Pure-Python fallbacks exist for some box math, but NMS and RoIAlign without the extension either fail or crawl. Second, the v1/v2 duality is genuine friction: both APIs live side by side, several v2 classes keep v1 aliases for backward compatibility, and v2 deliberately drops TorchScript support for containers like Compose — if your codebase still scripts transforms, migrating is a port, not a rename. Third, kernel coverage has edges: the CUDA NMS kernel targets standard boxes well, but rotated IoU and deformable paths are thinner (fewer tuned variants, occasional gaps on newer devices until the next release), and video transforms dispatch through fewer specialized kernels than their image counterparts. None of these are disqualifiers — they are the price of a Python API that compiles down to measured, device-specific kernels, and the reason torchvision remains the reference implementation the rest of the detection ecosystem measures against.
entry.summary: A source tour of torchvision: the transforms v2 engine, tv_tensors, and the NMS, RoIAlign, and deformable convolution C++/CUDA kernels behind detection models.

entry.title: XNNPACK Source Tour: The Microkernel Library Powering Mobile Inference

link.title: XNNPACK Source Tour: The Microkernel Library Powering Mobile Inference

entry.content:
If you have ever run a neural network on a phone, chances are the actual arithmetic was done by XNNPACK. It is the C library that sits underneath TensorFlow Lite, ExecuTorch, and the mobile builds of other runtimes, taking care of the least glamorous and most performance-critical part of inference: multiplying matrices with cache-friendly loops hand-tuned for each CPU flavor. Where engine-level projects like ONNX Runtime orchestrate graphs and devices, XNNPACK is the last mile — the layer where floats meet SIMD registers. And unlike GPU-oriented libraries such as ncnn (which also targets mobile, but with a Vulkan focus), XNNPACK is unapologetically CPU-first.

The library is famous for its brute-force thoroughness: hundreds of generated “microkernels”, one per tiling × ISA × data-type combination, dispatched at runtime to whatever your chip supports. The source is also a masterclass in systems design: above the kernels sits a declarative subgraph API, an optimizer that fuses nodes, a memory planner that schedules value lifetimes into one arena, and a weight-packing layer that reshapes constants into layouts the kernels can stream. This post walks that whole stack, from the public C API down to a generated NEON inner loop, using the current master tree as our map.

As always in this series, the code is the narrator: every symbol below links straight to the real line in the repository, and the diagrams were compiled from the actual file tree.

The XNNPACK flow at a glance: define nodes into a subgraph, build a runtime (which optimizes, plans memory, and packs weights), then invoke it so dispatch tables funnel packed data into ISA-specific microkernels.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • xnn_initialize, L47 — installs the process-wide allocator hooks and flips the global “initialized” bit that every later call checks.
  • xnn_subgraph_add_nodes, L352 — the single choke point through which every xnn_define_* call appends a node to the model.
  • xnn_define_convolution_2d, L1058 — the largest builder; validates shapes, padding, and grouping before recording a convolution node.
  • xnn_create_runtime_v4, L570 — the heavyweight constructor: optimizes the graph, plans memory, packs weights, and wires the executable operator chain.
  • xnn_plan_value_allocation_tracker, L210 — interval-schedules value lifetimes so all intermediates share one arena.
  • xnn_finalize_weights_cache, L514 — turns the packed-weights cache into a fixed, reusable memory region.
  • xnn_compute_gemm, L466 — the indirect-call glue that streams packed panels of weights and activations into a chosen ukernel.
  • xnn_init_f32_gemm_config, L7056 — scans a table of per-CPU candidates and returns the best GEMM configuration for this chip.
  • xnn_f32_gemm_minmax_ukernel_1x8__neon_dup_ld64, L21 — one of hundreds of generated microkernels: a 1×8-tile NEON GEMM inner loop.

A Subgraph, Not a Tensor Library

XNNPACK refuses to be a framework. There is no autograd, no device abstraction, no scheduler — you get two concepts: values and nodes. A value is a typed tensor with static dimensions; a node is an operator consuming and producing value IDs. Everything you build goes through xnn_define_tensor_value, L102, which registers a value and optionally hands back an external ID so the runtime can find it later, and then through builder functions like xnn_define_fully_connected, L1924 or xnn_define_batch_matrix_multiply, L620.

The builders are verbose by design — each one spends most of its lines on validation rather than work. xnn_define_convolution_2d, L1058 checks that padding is consistent, that group counts divide channel counts, and that the output dimensions are expressible at all, reusing helpers like xnn_compute_convolution_output_dimension, L46. This “fail loudly at build time” philosophy lets the hot path skip almost every check: by the time a kernel runs, the graph has been proven sane. Elementwise work gets the same treatment — xnn_define_binary, L175 and xnn_define_unary, L435 cover dozens of ops (add, multiply, relu, sigmoid, GELU, and friends) behind two functions, while xnn_define_softmax, L161 is a specialized node that will later be lowered to a fused exp / reduce-sum / divide chain.

This thin, explicit API is also why so many engines embed it. TensorFlow Lite’s delegate, ExecuTorch’s CPU backend, and mobile providers inside larger runtimes all translate their graph formats into these calls, keeping XNNPACK free of file-format or training opinions.

The Optimizer and the Memory Planner

Once the graph is complete, xnn_subgraph_optimize, L4853 runs a surprisingly long list of rewriting passes: merging adjacent reshapes, folding no-op binary ops, converting min/max pairs into clamps, simplifying negations, widening fp16 accumulators to fp32 when it changes accuracy, and even rewriting GEMMs whose right-hand side is transposed into a cheaper packing. None of this is optional polish — each pass removes work that would otherwise happen on every inference call.

Memory is planned with classic compiler techniques. populate_value_lifecycle, L37 records, for every intermediate value, the first and last node that touches it; xnn_plan_value_allocation_tracker, L210 then treats each value as an interval and packs the intervals into a single contiguous arena with minimal waste. Two tensors that never overlap in time can safely share bytes — on a phone, where 100 MB of activations is the difference between shipping and not shipping, this is not an optimization, it is a requirement. Allocation goes through the hooks installed by xnn_initialize, with defaults like xnn_allocate, L22 so an embedded target can swap in its own arena allocator.

Packing, Caching, and the Run Loop

The single most important idea in XNNPACK is that weights live in a different memory layout than on disk. GEMM kernels want fixed-size panels of rows so that each SIMD load streams contiguously; naive row-major weights would thrash the cache on every tile. So at setup time, every dense weight is repacked: the generic driver xnn_compute_packw_gemm_gio, L301 iterates over output-channel tiles, while the ISA-specific work happens in generated packers like xnn_x32_packw_gemm_goi_ukernel_x12__neon_ld4lane_u4, L20. Quantized dynamic GEMMs get a dedicated equivalent in xnn_pack_lh_f32_qdint8, L170, which pre-quantizes the left-hand side.

Repacking on every app start is wasteful. The weights cache solves this: xnn_internal_init_weights_cache, L281 creates a growable buffer, packed weights are written into it, and xnn_finalize_weights_cache, L514 seals it into a stable region that can be memoized and even serialized for the next launch. The underlying bytes come from xnn_allocate_weights_memory, L313, which allocates at page granularity and can drop write permission once packing is done — read-only packed weights are both safer and friendlier to the OS.

At run time, convolution-style operators use indirection tables instead of im2col: xnn_indirection_init_conv2d, L22 precomputes, for every output pixel and kernel tap, the pointer to the relevant input row. The kernels then just walk a table of pointers. xnn_invoke_runtime, L1238 walks the prepared operator list in topological order and each operator dispatches through function pointers like xnn_compute_gemm, which is where your float tensors finally meet SIMD.

Microkernels: Where the FLOPs Live

Every “compute” entry point ends in a microkernel — a fixed-tile function written in intrinsics or generated assembly. Selection is data-driven: init_hardware_config, L262 probes the CPU once (CPUID on x86, getauxval on Linux ARM); the resulting flags feed per-arch config tables such as xnn_init_f32_gemm_config, L7056, which chooses among a small forest of candidates. The naming encodes everything: f32-gemm-1x8-minmax-neon-dup-ld64 means fp32, 1×8 tile, min-max clamped, NEON with broadcast loads and 64-byte cache-line hints. Tile sizing is not arbitrary either — xnn_gemm_best_tile_size, L66 heuristically balances register pressure against weight reuse for small-M problems, which is exactly the regime mobile inference lives in.

Convolution gets direct kernels too: instead of lowering convolutions to GEMM, hot 3×3 cases run through specialized code like xnn_f32_conv_hwc_ukernel_3x3s2p1c3x8__aarch64_neonfma_2x2, L22, which processes the classic mobile conv directly in HWC layout, two output rows at a time. A look into the gen folders shows the scale: per-architecture .c and .S files for every tile × ISA × datatype combination, all produced by generator templates. Teardown is correspondingly tidy: xnn_delete_operator, L19 frees each operator through its type table, and the runtime releases the arena in one go.

From Install to Your First Model

XNNPACK is a C library, so “installation” means building it. The documented quick start uses CMake from the repo root (no official PyPI wheel exists, despite the abundance of xnnpack namesakes):

git clone https://github.com/google/XNNPACK.git
cd XNNPACK
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DXNNPACK_BUILD_TESTS=OFF
cmake --build build --config Release -j

scripts/build-local.sh wraps the same flow and adds a test run with CTest, and Bazel is supported equally well if that is your ecosystem. Link the resulting static library, include xnnpack.h, and a minimal fully-connected inference looks like this — the exact calls we verified in the tree above:

#include <xnnpack.h>

float input[8] = {/* ... */};
float filter[16], bias[4], output[4];  // 8 inputs -> 4 outputs

struct xnn_subgraph* subgraph = NULL;
struct xnn_runtime* runtime = NULL;
xnn_initialize(NULL /* default allocator */);

xnn_create_subgraph(2 /* external value ids */, 0 /* flags */, &subgraph);
const size_t in_dims[2] = {1, 8}, out_dims[2] = {1, 4};
uint32_t v_in, v_out;
xnn_define_tensor_value(subgraph, xnn_datatype_fp32, 2, in_dims,
                        NULL, 0 /* external id */, 0, &v_in);
xnn_define_tensor_value(subgraph, xnn_datatype_fp32, 2, out_dims,
                        NULL, 1 /* external id */, 0, &v_out);
xnn_define_fully_connected(subgraph, -INFINITY, INFINITY,
                           v_in, XNN_INVALID_VALUE_ID /* static filter */,
                           XNN_INVALID_VALUE_ID /* static bias */, v_out,
                           0 /* flags */);

xnn_create_runtime_v2(subgraph, NULL /* threadpool */, 0, &runtime);

For static weights you would instead define filter and bias values up front so the packer can process them at setup time. Setup binds real buffers, invoke runs, and teardown is two calls:

struct xnn_external_value ext[2] = {
    {0, input}, {1, output},
};
xnn_setup_runtime_v2(runtime, 2, ext);
xnn_invoke_runtime(runtime);
xnn_delete_runtime(runtime);
xnn_deinitialize();

The distinguishing trait versus, say, wrapping a model in TensorFlow Lite: you feel every tensor. Value IDs, dims, datatypes, and buffer bindings are all explicit. That is exactly what makes it such a predictable dependency for engines — and exactly what makes it tedious for humans. For a Python-flavored view of a runtime that makes different trade-offs on the same problem, see our earlier llama.cpp tour, and for how an engine composes providers around libraries like this one, see ONNX Runtime.

Honest Limits

  • The C API is loud. Building a real network means dozens of xnn_define_* calls with explicit IDs and dimension arrays. It is a kernel-target API, not an authoring API — you rarely write it directly; you generate it or delegate to it.
  • Inference only. There is no autodiff, no training path, no gradient of any kind. Quantization-aware tricks like fake-quant emulation are out of scope; you bring already-quantized weights.
  • Packing is format-locked. Packed weights are only meaningful to the library version that produced them; upgrading XNNPACK invalidates caches built with xnn_finalize_weights_cache, L514. The cache is also per-runtime-family — do not expect one buffer to serve arbitrary shapes.
  • Static shapes dominate. The fast path assumes fixed dims at build time; dynamic batch GEMM exists, but many rewrites and packings must be redone when shapes change, and xnn_reshape_runtime only covers a subset of cases cheaply.
  • Platform list is long but finite. Accelerated paths cover x86 (SSE/AVX/FMA3/AVX2/AVX512 and VNNI/BF16 variants), 32- and 64-bit ARM (NEON, dotprod, i8mm, bfloat16), RISC-V RVV, Hexagon HVX, and WASM SIMD. Everything else falls back to portable scalar code, which is correct but many times slower.
  • Threadpool coupling. Default parallelism assumes pthreadpool; wiring your own executor means threading it through every create call rather than a global setting.

None of these limits are accidents — they are the price of a library that treats a CPU’s cache hierarchy as the primary design constraint. That focus is why XNNPACK remains the default compute backend for on-device engines, and why its source still feels like a crash course in fast portable C: start at xnn_create_runtime_v4, L570, follow the packing into the gen folders, and you will never look at a matrix multiply the same way again.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of google/XNNPACK: the subgraph API, memory planner, weight packing, weights cache, and the CPU microkernels that make on-device inference fast.

entry.title: FasterTransformer Source Tour: The CUDA Kernel Lab Behind Modern LLM Serving

link.title: FasterTransformer Source Tour: The CUDA Kernel Lab Behind Modern LLM Serving

entry.content:
Between 2019 and 2022, if you wanted transformer inference to actually go fast on NVIDIA GPUs, you ended up reading FasterTransformer. It was NVIDIA’s C++/CUDA laboratory for the transformer block: attention, FFN, layernorm, sampling, and weight quantization treated as kernel-engineering problems rather than framework conveniences. It shipped encoder paths for BERT, decoder and decoding paths for machine translation, and a full GPT serving stack with bindings for TensorFlow, PyTorch, and a Triton backend. One honest note before anything else: the repository is frozen. The very first line of its README states that development has transitioned to TensorRT-LLM and that the repo “will not have further development.” Everything below should be read as a blueprint from that archive, not as a living project.

Why spend a post on frozen code? Because the blueprints escaped. The decode-time multi-head attention kernel we will visit is a direct ancestor of the one vLLM launched with, and its custom allreduce idea reappeared in TensorRT-LLM and vLLM almost unchanged in spirit. Its weight-only-quantization GEMM scaffolding, built on CUTLASS (a codebase we toured separately here), foreshadowed the entire W4A16 wave that ktransformers-style hybrid inference rides today. Reading FasterTransformer is reading the lab notebook that modern serving systems copied from.

This post walks the GPT serving path from a Triton model config down to a single CUDA kernel launch, using two diagrams generated directly from the src/fastertransformer tree on branch main: a compact overview first, and a detailed 34-node map later in the post. Every line anchor we link was verified against the working tree. If you want a warm-up on why token-level serving matters at all, our inference overview and the Triton Inference Server tour are good companions.

Overview of the FasterTransformer GPT serving stack: a Triton model builder instantiates the ParallelGpt engine, which drives context and step decoders over tensor-parallel attention and FFN layers, backed by fused kernels, custom allreduce, and a cuBLAS wrapper.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • ParallelGptTritonModel, L306 — the serving entry point; it parses a Triton config.ini, weights, and MPI world size, then spawns one engine per GPU and hands out model instances.
  • ParallelGpt::forward, L534 — the top-level engine loop: prefill over the prompt, then one step per generated token, sampling, stopping, and tensor-parallel logit gathers.
